sheet.howExamined: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. This is the first half of the logarithm question almost every year, worth 2 or 3 marks, and it is the part that separates the grades: Summer 2019 Q9(a) (most gave a ratio of logarithms and very few finished), Summer 2022 Q5(a) (which the report placed among the hardest questions that year), Summer 2023 Q7(a) (a good discriminator, only the best scored any marks), Summer 2024 Q6(a) (most lost the final mark), Summer 2025 Q9(a) (only a few reached the final answer). The Summer 2024 scheme gave M1 for the powers taken inside, M1 for the combining step and W1 for the finished single logarithm, with follow-through into the equation part that follows. Three of the last five papers set the laws part in a base other than ten (2022, 2023, 2026); the part after it is an indicial equation every year, and Summer 2019 joined the two with a one-line "show that" and a "hence".
traps: Writing log a + log b as log(a + b), so the plus goes inside unchanged
Writing log a − log b as log a ÷ log b, dividing the logarithms instead of the arguments (Summer 2025 FM1 Q9, Summer 2019 FM1 Q9)
Applying a coefficient to the variable but not to its number, so 3 log 2x becomes log 2x³ (Summer 2024 FM1 Q6)
Taking a coefficient inside as a multiplier rather than as a power, so 3 log x becomes log 3x
Putting a subtracted term in the numerator, or an added one in the denominator (Summer 2025 FM1 Q9)
Being unable to split a product or a quotient into separate logarithms at all (Summer 2022 FM1 Q5)
Not seeing how to build a number from the logarithms given, such as 10.5 from logs of 2, 3 and 7 (Summer 2023 FM1 Q7)
Reaching log y² = log x³ and stopping, instead of dropping the logarithms (Summer 2019 FM1 Q9)
Dropping the bracket when a built logarithm such as 1 − q is substituted, so p + q − (1 − q) is written p + q − 1 − q
Combining constants and roots wrongly inside a single logarithm (Summer 2025 FM1 Q9)
Leaving the bracket off when a whole expression comes down as a coefficient, writing 2x − 1 log 3 where (2x − 1) log 3 is meant (Summer 2018 FM1 Q6)
Treating log as a number to divide by, which leaves a ratio of logarithms instead of an equation in y and x; it was the most common answer that year (Summer 2019 FM1 Q9)
Reaching for logarithms when both sides are already powers of the same number, where comparing the indices finishes the job at once (Summer 2019 FM1 Q9)
Not using the result of a "show that" part in the "hence" part straight after it (Summer 2019 FM1 Q9)

noteBlocks.lede: A logarithm counts powers of ten, so it turns multiplying into adding. Three laws follow, and they run both ways: squeeze several logarithms into one, or open one into several. Every laws question on the paper is one of those two jobs, sometimes in a base other than ten.
can: Combine several logarithms into one, coefficients, numbers and roots included
Expand one logarithm, or write it in terms of the logarithms you are given
Solve log P = log Q, and write one letter in terms of another

noteBlocks.md: Multiplying adds steps, and that one fact gives the three laws of the next three sections. Each works forwards, squeezing logarithms into one, or backwards, opening one out.

steps.decision: Count the steps of ten from $1$: there are four.
A number below $1$ sits to the left of $1$: three steps the other way, so its logarithm is negative.

noteBlocks.explain: $100\,000 = 10^{5}$: five steps of ten from $1$, so its logarithm is $5$. This is step 1 of See it.

twin.explain: $0.01 = 10^{-2}$: two steps to the left of $1$, so its logarithm is $-2$.

noteBlocks.md:
$\log a + \log b = \log(ab)$. The plus sign outside becomes a times sign inside; it never goes in as a plus.
The ruler shows why. The hop for $4$ is $0.602$ and the hop for $25$ is $1.398$, and together they reach $2$, which is where $100$ sits.

noteBlocks.stem: Write $\log 4 + \log 25$ as a single logarithm, and find its value.

steps.decision: Adding outside multiplies inside.
$100 = 10^{2}$, so the single logarithm is exactly $2$, as the two hops showed.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $\log 6 + \log 7$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: Adding the numbers inside is the slip to watch: the plus outside becomes a times inside, so it is $\log 42$.
That multiplies the logarithms themselves; the law multiplies the numbers inside one logarithm, $\log(6 \times 7)$.

noteBlocks.explain: Adding outside multiplies inside: $\log 6 + \log 7 = \log(6 \times 7) = \log 42$. This is step 1 of See it.

optionNotes.why: Adding the numbers inside is the slip to watch: the plus outside becomes a times inside, so it is $\log 39$.

noteBlocks.md:
$\log a - \log b = \log\frac{a}{b}$. The minus goes inside as a division.
It is not $\frac{\log a}{\log b}$, which divides the logarithms themselves: $\log 100 \div \log 4$ is about $3.32$, and that is not the logarithm of anything here.

steps.decision: Subtracting outside divides inside.
Simplify the fraction inside: the answer is still one logarithm.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $\log 12 - \log 3$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: That subtracts the numbers inside; subtracting logarithms divides inside, so it is $\log\frac{12}{3}$.
That divides the logarithms themselves; the division belongs inside one logarithm.

noteBlocks.explain: Subtracting outside divides inside, so it is $\log\frac{12}{3} = \log 4$. Dividing the two logarithms is a different calculation altogether. This is step 1 of See it.

noteBlocks.md: $n\log a = \log a^{n}$. The coefficient climbs inside as an index, and the index lands on **everything** inside: when the inside is a bracket such as $4x$, the number is raised as well as the letter, as the sixteen small squares show.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024, Unit 1, Question 6
noteBlocks.md: Marks went on the last step. Raising a bracket with a number in it, most candidates raised the letter and forgot the number. Write the bracket out before you expand it, every time.

steps.decision: The coefficient becomes an index on the whole bracket.
The square lands on the $4$ as well as on the $x$.
One logarithm, with the bracket multiplied out.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $2\log 3x$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The square reached the $x$ but not the $3$; $(3x)^{2}$ squares both, giving $9x^{2}$.
The $2$ went inside as a multiplier; a coefficient goes inside as a power, so it is $(3x)^{2}$.

noteBlocks.explain: $2\log 3x = \log\left((3x)^{2}\right)$, and $(3x)^{2} = 9x^{2}$: the square lands on the $3$ as well as the $x$. This is steps 1 and 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: What is $3\log 5x$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The cube reached the $x$ but not the $5$; $(5x)^{3}$ cubes both, giving $125x^{3}$.
The $3$ went inside as a multiplier; a coefficient goes inside as a power, so it is $(5x)^{3}$.

noteBlocks.md:
Every law is one fact about the ruler: multiplying by $b$ is always the same hop, $\log b$, wherever you start.
So a product is a sum of hops, and a division is a hop back. A power repeats one hop: $a^{3} = a \times a \times a$ is three hops of $\log a$, so $\log a^{3} = 3\log a$.

noteBlocks.title: Why the laws never change
noteBlocks.md: A logarithm is an index, and the laws are the index laws read the other way: multiply two powers of ten and the indices add. The index laws hold in every base, so these laws do too.

noteBlocks.stem: Given that $\log 3 = 0.477$ to 3 decimal places, find $\log 3000$ and $\log 27$.

steps.decision: Multiplying by $1000$ is three more steps of ten.
A cube is three hops of $\log 3$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Given that $\log 2 = 0.301$ to 3 decimal places, what is $\log 200$ to 3 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: $200 = 2 \times 100$, and multiplying by $100$ is two more steps of ten, so $\log 200 = 0.301 + 2 = 2.301$. This is step 1 of See it.

twin.prompt: Given that $\log 7 = 0.845$ to 3 decimal places, what is $\log 700$ to 3 decimal places?
twin.explain: $700 = 7 \times 100$: two more steps of ten, so $\log 700 = 0.845 + 2 = 2.845$.

noteBlocks.md: To write several logarithms as one, work in a fixed order. Coefficients become powers first. Then the added terms multiply on top, and the subtracted terms go underneath.
If the argument then simplifies, simplify it: $\log\frac{9x^{2}}{3x}$ is $\log 3x$. Putting a term on the wrong side of the line is a slip the Summer 2025 report names.

noteBlocks.stem: Write $\log u + 2\log v - 4\log w$ as a single logarithm.

steps.decision: Coefficients become powers first.
The added terms multiply.
The subtracted term goes underneath.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $3\log h + \log k - 2\log m$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The $k$ was added, so it belongs on top with $h^{3}$; only the subtracted term goes underneath.
The coefficients went in as multipliers; each becomes a power first, so $3\log h$ is $\log h^{3}$.

noteBlocks.explain: Powers first: $\log h^{3} + \log k - \log m^{2}$. The added terms multiply on top and the subtracted one goes underneath: $\log\frac{h^{3}k}{m^{2}}$. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it.

twin.prompt: What is $\log s + 4\log t - 3\log n$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The $s$ was added, so it belongs on top with $t^{4}$; only the subtracted term goes underneath.
The coefficients went in as multipliers; each becomes a power first, so $4\log t$ is $\log t^{4}$.

twin.explain: Powers first, then multiply the added terms on top and put the subtracted one underneath: $\log\frac{st^{4}}{n^{3}}$.

noteBlocks.md: The laws only combine logarithms, so a bare number must become one first. To base ten, $1 = \log 10$ and $3 = \log 1000$, so $3 + \log x$ becomes $\log 1000 + \log x$, which is $\log 1000x$.

A root is a power too: $\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}$, so $\frac{1}{2}\log x = \log\sqrt{x}$.
With a coefficient in front, multiply the powers: $6\log\sqrt{c} = \log c^{3}$, because $6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3$. The Summer 2025 report found numbers and roots combined wrongly.

steps.decision: The bare number becomes a logarithm first.
$\sqrt{y} = y^{\frac{1}{2}}$, and $4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 2$.
Now the product law combines them as usual.

noteBlocks.prompt: To base $10$, what is $\log h - 1$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The $1$ went inside as a number; it has to become $\log 10$ first, and subtracting a logarithm divides.
The fraction is upside down: $\log 10$ is the term being subtracted, so the $10$ goes underneath.

noteBlocks.explain: $1 = \log 10$, so $\log h - 1 = \log h - \log 10 = \log\frac{h}{10}$. This is step 1 of See it, then the quotient law.

twin.prompt: To base $10$, what is $\log y - 2$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The $2$ went inside as a number; it has to become $\log 100$ first, and subtracting a logarithm divides.
The fraction is upside down: $\log 100$ is the term being subtracted, so the $100$ goes underneath.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $8\log\sqrt{y}$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The $8$ went inside as a multiplier; it becomes a power, and $8 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4$.
The root was treated as a square; $\sqrt{y}$ is $y^{\frac{1}{2}}$, so the powers multiply to $4$, not $16$.

noteBlocks.explain: $\sqrt{y} = y^{\frac{1}{2}}$, and $8 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4$, so it is $\log y^{4}$. Squaring instead of halving gives $y^{16}$. This is step 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: What is $12\log\sqrt{z}$ as a single logarithm?

optionNotes.why: The $12$ went inside as a multiplier; it becomes a power, and $12 \times \frac{1}{2} = 6$.
The root was treated as a square; $\sqrt{z}$ is $z^{\frac{1}{2}}$, so the powers multiply to $6$, not $24$.

twin.explain: $\sqrt{z} = z^{\frac{1}{2}}$, and $12 \times \frac{1}{2} = 6$, so it is $\log z^{6}$.

noteBlocks.md:
Some questions want one logarithm opened into several. Run the laws from right to left: a product splits into a sum, a quotient into a difference, and each power drops in front.
$\log\frac{a^{5}}{b^{3}}$ splits into $\log a^{5} - \log b^{3}$, which is $5\log a - 3\log b$. A square root drops in as $\frac{1}{2}$.

steps.decision: The quotient splits first.
All of the denominator is subtracted: the product splits, and both parts are taken away.
Each power drops in front, the root as $\frac{1}{2}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $\log(h^{5}k)$ written as separate logarithms?

optionNotes.why: A product splits into a sum of logarithms, not a product of them.
The power belongs to $h$ and drops in front as a coefficient: $5\log h$, not $\log 5h$.

noteBlocks.explain: The product splits into a sum, $\log h^{5} + \log k$, then the power drops in front: $5\log h + \log k$. This is steps 2 and 3 of See it.

twin.prompt: What is $\log(r^{6}s)$ written as separate logarithms?

optionNotes.why: A product splits into a sum of logarithms, not a product of them.
The power belongs to $r$ and drops in front as a coefficient: $6\log r$, not $\log 6r$.

noteBlocks.md: Once an equation reads $\log P = \log Q$, the logarithms can go: $P = Q$. Make each side a single logarithm first.
The same step writes one letter in terms of another. From $2\log y = 5\log x$, the power law gives $\log y^{2} = \log x^{5}$, so $y^{2} = x^{5}$ and $y = x^{\frac{5}{2}}$.

steps.decision: Make the left side one logarithm.
Equal logarithms have equal arguments.
Check it: $\log 7 + \log 3 = \log 21$.

noteBlocks.explain: Combine: $\log 6x = \log 54$, so $6x = 54$ and $x = 9$. Writing $x + 6 = 54$ adds inside and gives $48$. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it.

noteBlocks.md: Told that $\log 2 = u$ and $\log 5 = v$, you can reach any number built from twos and fives. Factorise it first: $50 = 2 \times 5^{2}$, so $\log 50 = \log 2 + 2\log 5$, which is $u + 2v$.
A number outside your factors may still be reached through $10$, because $\log 10 = 1$: with only $\log 2 = u$, write $5 = \frac{10}{2}$, so $\log 5 = 1 - u$.

noteBlocks.stem: Given that $\log 2 = u$ and $\log 7 = w$, express $\log 5.6$ in terms of $u$ and $w$.

steps.decision: Write it with the numbers you have, and a power of ten.
Product to sum, quotient to difference, power in front.
$\log 10 = 1$ to base ten.

noteBlocks.prompt: Given that $\log 2 = u$ and $\log 3 = w$, what is $\log 54$ in terms of $u$ and $w$?

optionNotes.why: The index stayed on the letter; the power law brings it down in front, so $\log 3^{3} = 3\log 3 = 3w$.
$54 = 2 \times 3^{3}$ is a product, so the logarithms add: $u + 3w$, not a product of the letters.

noteBlocks.explain: $54 = 2 \times 3^{3}$, so $\log 54 = \log 2 + 3\log 3 = u + 3w$. This is steps 1 and 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: Given that $\log 2 = u$ and $\log 7 = w$, what is $\log 28$ in terms of $u$ and $w$?

optionNotes.why: The index stayed on the letter; the power law brings it down in front, so $\log 2^{2} = 2\log 2 = 2u$.
$28 = 2^{2} \times 7$ is a product, so the logarithms add: $2u + w$, not a product of the letters.

noteBlocks.md: The laws hold in every base, and the base's own logarithm is $1$: $\log_{5} 5 = 1$. So the base is the one number whose logarithm needs no letter, and it is worth looking for as a factor before anything else.

noteBlocks.stem: Given that $\log_{5} 2 = t$, express $\log_{5} 12.5$ in terms of $t$.

steps.decision: Factor out the base.
The quotient becomes a difference.

noteBlocks.prompt: Given that $\log_{5} 2 = t$, what is $\log_{5} 50$ in terms of $t$?

optionNotes.why: $\log_{5} 25$ is the power of $5$ that gives $25$, which is $2$, not $25$ itself.
$25 \div 5 = 5$ divides instead of asking for the power: $5^{2} = 25$, so $\log_{5} 25 = 2$.

noteBlocks.explain: $50 = 2 \times 5^{2}$, so $\log_{5} 50 = \log_{5} 2 + 2 = t + 2$: the base's own power gives a plain $2$. This is steps 1 and 3 of See it.

twin.prompt: Given that $\log_{5} 2 = t$, what is $\log_{5} 250$ in terms of $t$?

optionNotes.why: $\log_{5} 125$ is the power of $5$ that gives $125$, which is $3$, not $125$ itself.
$125 \div 5 = 25$ divides instead of asking for the power: $5^{3} = 125$, so $\log_{5} 125 = 3$.

noteBlocks.md: **$x$ in the indices** (every paper, 2018 to 2026). The partner part is an equation with $x$ in two indices: take logarithms of both sides, and each index comes down whole, in a bracket. **A base other than ten** (2022, 2023, 2026): the laws are unchanged, and the base's own logarithm is $1$.
**A coefficient on a bracket or a root** (2024, 2025). The power reaches everything inside: $2\log 7x = \log 49x^{2}$ and $10\log\sqrt{c} = \log c^{5}$.
**One letter in terms of another** (2019, 2021). Make each side a single logarithm, or write both letters as multiples of one shared logarithm, then compare.

noteBlocks.stem: Given that $y = \log 9$ and $z = \log 27$, express $z$ in terms of $y$.

steps.decision: Write each letter as a multiple of one shared logarithm.
The same shared logarithm, $\log 3$.
Remove the shared logarithm between the two lines.

noteBlocks.prompt: Given that $p = \log 4$ and $q = \log 32$, what is $q$ in terms of $p$?

optionNotes.why: That divides the numbers inside, $32 \div 4 = 8$; compare the logarithms instead: $p = 2\log 2$ and $q = 5\log 2$.
The ratio is upside down: $\log 2 = \frac{p}{2}$, so $q = 5 \times \frac{p}{2}$.

noteBlocks.explain: $p = \log 2^{2} = 2\log 2$ and $q = \log 2^{5} = 5\log 2$. So $\log 2 = \frac{p}{2}$ and $q = \frac{5p}{2}$. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it.

twin.prompt: Given that $m = \log 25$ and $n = \log 125$, what is $n$ in terms of $m$?

optionNotes.why: That divides the numbers inside, $125 \div 25 = 5$; compare the logarithms instead: $m = 2\log 5$ and $n = 3\log 5$.
The ratio is upside down: $\log 5 = \frac{m}{2}$, so $n = 3 \times \frac{m}{2}$.

noteBlocks.md:
The laws turn a curve into a straight line. Take logarithms of $y = kx^{n}$: the product law splits the right side and the power law brings $n$ down, so $\log y = n\log x + \log k$.
That is a line with gradient $n$ and intercept $\log k$. The papers set it every year from 2018 to 2025, and the log/log graphs lesson takes it from here.

noteBlocks.title: Where the specification stops
noteBlocks.md: The change of base rule, natural logarithms and the number $e$ are not on this specification. Every logarithm here is to base ten or to a base the question states.

noteBlocks.stem: If $y = 2x^{4}$, write $\log y$ in terms of $\log x$.

steps.decision: The product law splits the right side.
The power law brings the $4$ down, onto $\log x$ alone.

optionNotes.why: The $3$ belongs to $x$ alone; $3\log 5x$ would cube the $5$ as well.
The $5$ stays inside a logarithm: the product law gives $\log 5$, not $5$.

noteBlocks.explain: The product law splits $5x^{3}$ into $\log 5 + \log x^{3}$, and the power law brings the $3$ down. The $3$ belongs to $x$ alone, so $\log 5$ keeps no coefficient. This is steps 1 and 2 of See it.

optionNotes.why: The $2$ belongs to $x$ alone; $2\log 7x$ would square the $7$ as well.
The $7$ stays inside a logarithm: the product law gives $\log 7$, not $7$.

noteBlocks.md:
Let $a = 10^{p}$ and $b = 10^{q}$, so that $p = \log a$ and $q = \log b$.
Then $ab = 10^{p + q}$, because indices add, so the logarithm of the product is $p + q$: the product law.
Nothing here needs base ten: put any base in place of $10$ and every line still holds.

steps.decision: Write each number as a power of ten; then $p = \log a$ and $q = \log b$.
Dividing powers of ten subtracts the indices.
Read the index back as a logarithm.

noteBlocks.prompt: Let $a = 10^{p}$. What is $\log a^{3}$ in terms of $p$?

optionNotes.why: Cubing $a$ multiplies its index by $3$: $(10^{p})^{3} = 10^{3p}$, so the logarithm is $3p$.
Adding $3$ to the index would multiply $a$ by $1000$; cubing multiplies the index instead.

noteBlocks.explain: $a^{3} = (10^{p})^{3} = 10^{3p}$, so $\log a^{3} = 3p$, which is $3\log a$: the power law, derived the way step 2 of See it derived the quotient law.

twin.prompt: Let $b = 10^{q}$. What is $\log b^{5}$ in terms of $q$?

optionNotes.why: Raising $b$ to the fifth multiplies its index by $5$: $(10^{q})^{5} = 10^{5q}$, so the logarithm is $5q$.
Adding $5$ to the index would multiply $b$ by $100\,000$; the power multiplies the index instead.

noteBlocks.md:
Combine logarithms: coefficients to powers, then add, then subtract.
Put numbers and roots inside, as logarithms and as powers.
Expand one logarithm, or write it in terms of the ones you are given.
Drop the logarithms from $\log P = \log Q$, and write one letter in terms of another.
Spot the twists: a bracket or a root under a coefficient, a new base, $x$ in the indices.

Expect a laws part worth $2$ or $3$ marks, then an indicial equation. The first mark is usually the coefficients written as powers; the last is one logarithm, or the expression in the given letters. A "show that" line is there to be used in the part after it. Stuck? Coefficients first, then add, then subtract.

Because the coefficient can be cancelled from every term
Because a coefficient multiplies the argument

options.feedback: Everything inside the bracket is cubed, so the $2$ becomes $8$.
Only the $x$ has been cubed. The bracket means the $2$ is cubed as well.
The $2$ has been multiplied by $3$ rather than cubed.

items.skill: Evaluating a logarithm from a power

options.feedback: $10^{2} = 100$, so the logarithm is $2$. That fact is what lets a constant be written as a logarithm.
That is the base. The logarithm is the index on the base.
That is the number inside. The answer is the index that reaches it.

items.stem: Write $7.5$ as a fraction, fully simplified.
items.skill: Turning a decimal into a fraction

options.feedback: $7.5 = \frac{15}{2}$, and $15 = 3 \times 5$, which is where the given logarithms come in.
The digits have been read as a fraction. $7.5$ is seven and a half.
That is $0.75$. The number here is larger than $7$.

items.stem: What is $\log 5 + \log 6$ as a single logarithm?

options.feedback: Adding logarithms multiplies the arguments.
The plus has gone inside unchanged. Added outside means multiplied inside.
The logarithms themselves are not multiplied. One logarithm of the product is what the law gives.

items.stem: What is $\log 20 - \log 4$ as a single logarithm?

options.feedback: Subtracting outside divides inside: $\log\frac{20}{4} = \log 5$.
The minus has gone inside unchanged. Subtracted outside means divided inside.
Dividing the two logarithms is a different calculation, and it is not the logarithm of anything here.

items.stem: What is $4\log 3x$ as a single logarithm?
items.skill: The power law with a coefficient inside

options.feedback: $(3x)^{4} = 81x^{4}$: the fourth power reaches the $3$ as well.
The power reached the $x$ but not the $3$. Write the bracket $(3x)^{4}$ first.
The $4$ has gone inside as a multiplier rather than as a power.

items.stem: Where does the $c$ go when $\log a + \log b - \log c$ is written as a single logarithm?

options.feedback: A subtracted logarithm divides, so its argument goes underneath.
The subtracted term is $c$, so $c$ is the one that divides. Check which term carries the minus.
The division happens inside one logarithm, not outside it.

items.stem: To base $10$, what is $1 + \log x$ as a single logarithm?
items.skill: A constant written as a logarithm

options.feedback: $1 = \log 10$, and then the product law gives $\log 10x$.
The $1$ has gone inside as an addition. It first has to become $\log 10$.
The $1$ cannot simply be dropped. It is $\log 10$, and it multiplies inside.

items.stem: An equation has reached $\log 4x = \log 20$. What comes next?

options.feedback: Equal logarithms have equal arguments, so the logarithms are dropped together.
Nothing needs dividing here. Both sides are already single logarithms.

options.text: It cannot be taken any further without a calculator

parts.stem:
When $v = 5$, $P = 250$, and when $v = 10$, $P = 2000$.
Use your answer to part (a) to find the value of $n$.

From part (a): $\log 250 = \log k + n\log 5$ and $\log 2000 = \log k + n\log 10$.
Subtracting: $\log 2000 - \log 250 = n(\log 10 - \log 5)$.
The quotient law gives $\log 8 = n\log 2$.
Since $8 = 2^{3}$, $n = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the change in $\log v$ divided by the change in $\log P$, which is upside down. $n$ multiplies $\log v$, so $n = \frac{\log 8}{\log 2} = 3$.

parts.stem: Find the value of $k$.

So $k = 2$.

context.setting: An expansion, a rearrangement and an equation with a root to reject

parts.stem:
Express $\log\frac{x^{2}\sqrt{y}}{z^{3}}$ as separate logarithms.
Give your answer as separate logarithms.
hints: Split the division first.
A square root is a power of $\frac{1}{2}$.
parts.workedSolution:
The division splits first: $\log(x^{2}\sqrt{y}) - \log z^{3}$.
The product splits next, and each power drops down: $2\log x + \frac{1}{2}\log y - 3\log z$.

commonErrors.feedback: The square root has been dropped rather than brought down as a half. A root is a power of $\frac{1}{2}$, so that term is $\frac{1}{2}\log y$.

parts.stem:
It is given that $3\log x = 2\log z$.
Express $x$ in terms of $z$.
hints: Take both coefficients inside as powers, then drop the logarithms.
parts.workedSolution:
The power law gives $\log x^{3} = \log z^{2}$, so $x^{3} = z^{2}$.
Taking the cube root, $x = z^{\frac{2}{3}}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The logarithm was left on one side. Once both sides are single logarithms they can be dropped, giving $x^{3} = z^{2}$.

parts.stem:
Solve the equation
$\log(x + 2) + \log(x - 2) = \log 12$
hints: Combine the left side into one logarithm.
Both roots of $x^{2} = 16$ must be tested in the original equation.
parts.workedSolution:
Combining the left side: $\log\left((x + 2)(x - 2)\right) = \log 12$.
Equal logarithms have equal arguments, so $(x + 2)(x - 2) = 12$ and $x^{2} - 4 = 12$.
So $x^{2} = 16$ and $x = 4$ or $x = -4$.
At $x = -4$ the expression $\log(x - 2)$ has a negative argument, so that root is rejected and $x = 4$.

commonErrors.feedback: The left side was read as $\log(2x)$, adding inside instead of multiplying. Multiplying the brackets gives $x^{2} - 4 = 12$ and $x = 4$.
Both roots of $x^{2} = 16$ are there, but $x = -4$ has to be rejected: it makes both brackets negative, $-2$ and $-6$, and there is no logarithm of a negative number. The answer is $x = 4$ only.

parts.stem: Express $2\log 6x - \log 4x$ as a single logarithm.
hints: Write the bracket before you square it.
The subtracted term goes underneath, then cancel inside.
parts.workedSolution:
The coefficient becomes a power on the whole bracket: $2\log 6x = \log 36x^{2}$.
Subtracting divides inside: $\log\frac{36x^{2}}{4x}$.
Cancelling inside, the single logarithm is $\log 9x$.

commonErrors.feedback: The square reached the $x$ but not the $6$. The whole bracket is squared, $(6x)^{2} = 36x^{2}$, which leaves $\log 9x$.

The fraction is upside down. The term with the minus, $\log 4x$, is the one that goes underneath.

parts.stem:

hints: Factorise $48$ with the base, $2$, as a factor.

parts.stem:
Write $8 \times 2^{x}$ in the form $2^{x + a}$.
Write down the value of $a$.
hints: Write $8$ as a power of $2$.
Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices.
parts.workedSolution:
$8 = 2^{3}$, so $8 \times 2^{x} = 2^{3} \times 2^{x}$.
The indices add: $2^{x + 3}$, so $a = 3$.

parts.stem:
Hence solve the equation
$5^{2x - 1} = 8 \times 2^{x}$
Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
hints: Use part (c) to write the right-hand side as one power of $2$.
Take logarithms of both sides, keeping each index in a bracket.
parts.workedSolution:
By part (c), the equation is $5^{2x - 1} = 2^{x + 3}$.
Taking logarithms: $(2x - 1)\log 5 = (x + 3)\log 2$.
Expanding: $2x\log 5 - \log 5 = x\log 2 + 3\log 2$.
Gathering the $x$ terms: $x(2\log 5 - \log 2) = 3\log 2 + \log 5$.
So $x = 1.4605$, which is $1.46$ to 2 decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: The brackets went missing when the indices came down, so only the $1$ and the $3$ met the logarithms. Write $(2x - 1)\log 5 = (x + 3)\log 2$ first; the answer is $1.46$.
The $x\log 2$ term crossed to the left without its sign changing. Gathering the $x$ terms gives $x(2\log 5 - \log 2)$, and the answer is $1.46$.

context.setting: Two logarithms to base 2 equal to a number: the laws make one logarithm and the index form finishes it

parts.stem:
Solve the equation
$\log_{2} x + \log_{2}(x + 2) = 3$
hints: Combine the left side into one logarithm first.
Nothing on the right is a logarithm, so write the equation in index form: a logarithm to base $2$ equal to $3$ means the number inside is $2^{3}$.
Test both roots in the original equation: a logarithm needs a positive number.
parts.workedSolution:
Combining the left side: $\log_{2}\left(x(x + 2)\right) = 3$.
In index form, $x(x + 2) = 2^{3} = 8$, so $x^{2} + 2x - 8 = 0$.
That factorises as $(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0$, so $x = 2$ or $x = -4$.
At $x = -4$ the term $\log_{2} x$ has a negative argument, so that root is rejected and $x = 2$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two logarithms were added inside, as $\log_{2}(2x + 2)$. Added logarithms multiply inside: $\log_{2}\left(x(x + 2)\right) = 3$, so $x(x + 2) = 8$ and $x = 2$.
The logarithm was undone by multiplying the base by the $3$, giving $x(x + 2) = 6$. The index form raises the base to that power instead: $x(x + 2) = 2^{3} = 8$, and then $x = 2$.
Both roots of $x^{2} + 2x - 8 = 0$ are there, but $x = -4$ has to be rejected: $\log_{2} x$ has no value at a negative number. The answer is $x = 2$ only.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife was asked to express $3\log 2x$ as a single logarithm. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are exactly right: the coefficient is inside and the bracket is there, which is the first mark.
Line 3 expands the bracket as though the cube belonged to the $x$ alone. $(2x)^{3}$ means $2x \times 2x \times 2x$, so the $2$ is cubed as well: $(2x)^{3} = 8x^{3}$.
Check it on a number. At $x = 1.5$, $3\log 2x = 1.431364$ and $\log 8x^{3} = 1.431364$, while $\log 2x^{3} = 0.829304$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The bracket was written, so the first mark stands. What went are the last two marks, and the step that lost them is the one the Summer 2024 report says the majority got wrong. When you expand a bracket with a power, say the coefficient out loud first: two cubed is eight.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruairí was asked to solve $\log(x + 5) - \log(x - 1) = \log 3$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 3, 4 and 5 are all correct work, and the final answer happens to be right.
Line 2 is not. It divides one logarithm by the other, which is a different quantity from $\log\frac{x + 5}{x - 1}$. The line that belongs there is $\log\frac{x + 5}{x - 1} = \log 3$: subtracting logarithms divides inside one logarithm, not outside.
A right answer reached through a wrong line still loses the method mark, because the examiner marks the working.
findTheMistake.feedback: Everything after line 2 is sound, so most of the marks stand. The quotient law puts the division inside the logarithm, and the difference matters: $\log 100 - \log 4$ is $\log 25$, while $\log 100 \div \log 4$ is about $3.321928$. Write the single logarithm before you drop it.

findTheMistake.stem: Méabh was asked to express $\log a + 2\log b - \log c$ as a single logarithm. Her working:
studentWorking: log a + 2 log b - log c
= log a + log b^2 - log c
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are right: the coefficient has gone inside as a power, which is the first mark.
Line 3 gathers the wrong pair. The minus sign belongs to $\log c$, so it is $c$ that divides, and $b^{2}$ that multiplies. The line should read $\log(ab^{2}) - \log c$.
The finished single logarithm is $\log\frac{ab^{2}}{c}$, with the subtracted term underneath.
findTheMistake.feedback: The power law was applied correctly and that mark stands. Before you combine, underline the term that carries the minus: that one, and only that one, goes underneath. The Summer 2025 report names this swap directly.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara was asked to solve $3^{x + 1} = 40$, giving $x$ correct to 2 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 is right: taking logarithms of both sides is the first mark.
Line 2 brings the index down without its bracket. The power law brings down the whole index, $x + 1$, so the line must read $(x + 1)\log 3 = \log 40$. Without the bracket only the $1$ meets $\log 3$, and line 3 follows that misreading.
With the bracket, $x + 1 = \frac{\log 40}{\log 3}$, so $x = 2.36$.
findTheMistake.feedback: Taking logarithms was right, and that mark stands. The Summer 2018 report singled out this slip: brackets left off when an index comes down. Write the bracket the moment the index moves, before anything else.

prompts.prompt: Write the three laws of logarithms.
prompts.answer: $\log a + \log b = \log(ab)$, $\log a - \log b = \log\frac{a}{b}$, and $n\log a = \log a^{n}$.

prompts.prompt: What is $\log a + \log b$, and what is it not?
prompts.answer: It is $\log(ab)$. It is not $\log(a + b)$: the plus outside becomes a times inside.

prompts.prompt: What is $\log a - \log b$, and what is it not?
prompts.answer: It is $\log\frac{a}{b}$. It is not $\frac{\log a}{\log b}$: the division happens inside one logarithm.

prompts.prompt: In what order do you combine several logarithms into one?
prompts.answer: Coefficients first, turning each into a power; then add the terms to multiply inside; then subtract, putting that argument underneath.

prompts.prompt: To base $10$, how do you write the number $2$ as a logarithm?
prompts.answer: $2 = \log 100$, because $10^{2} = 100$. A constant has to become a logarithm before the laws can combine it.

prompts.prompt: How do you expand $\log\frac{x^{3}}{y}$ into separate logarithms?
prompts.answer: The division becomes a subtraction and the power drops down: $3\log x - \log y$.

prompts.prompt: An equation has reached $\log P = \log Q$. What can you do?
prompts.answer: Drop both logarithms: $P = Q$. Each side must be a single logarithm first.

prompts.prompt: In any base $b$, what is $\log_{b} b$?
prompts.answer: It is 1, because $b^{1} = b$: each factor of the base gives 1.

findings.wentWrong: Mostly right; careless bracket omission (2x - 1 log 3), and bases other than 10 produced more slips; isolating x was the hurdle for the rest.
findings.rule: Write (2x - 1) log 3 with brackets; keep calculator work to the last step.

findings.asked: Combine logs to express y in terms of x; solve an indicial equation.
findings.wentWrong: Many wrote the ratio of logs instead of combining; some reached log y squared = log x cubed and y squared = x cubed but almost none finished with y = x to the three halves. In (b) indices were rarely used and the log route stalled.
findings.rule: n log a = log a to the n; equal logs mean equal arguments.

findings.asked: Split the log of a product/quotient into separate logs; solve a log equation.
findings.wentWrong: Very few could separate the expression into a sum of logs even when they knew a sum was expected. The equation was fine, apart from moving the x terms.
findings.rule: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a - log b.

findings.asked: Express a log of a number in terms of given logs.
findings.wentWrong: Only the best saw how to build 10.5 from 2, 3 and 7.
findings.rule: Factorise the number into the given bases (10.5 = 3 x 7 / 2).

findings.asked: Simplify a log expression involving 3 log 2x.
findings.wentWrong: The majority forgot to cube the 2 when writing 3 log 2x as a single log.

findings.asked: Write an expression as a single log; solve a log equation.
findings.wentWrong: Constants and roots were combined wrongly, a subtracted term's variable was put in the denominator incorrectly (or an added one), and the subtraction rule was misapplied; the equation part was strong.
findings.rule: Added logs multiply inside; subtracted logs divide; coefficients become powers first.

insight.ruleToRemember: log a + log b = log ab, log a - log b = log(a/b), n log a = log a to the n (apply the power to the whole argument, coefficient included); once you have log P = log Q, write P = Q.
